To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

herbivory by Zeira canadensis on white spruce induces the formation of new buds at the base of damaged shoots and that this response improves the synchrony of bud development with egg hatch in the year following attack.

herbivory by a folivore of early season white spruce buds induced a shift in the phenological timing of bud development, which in turn improved the synchrony of larval emergence and bud burst in the subsequent spring, thereby increasing the survival of larvae.

herbivory by the bud moth, Zeiraphera canadensis (Lepidopteran: Tortricidae) induces ameliorative changes in the phenology and morphology of white spruce, Picea glauca (Coniferan: Pinaceae), that improve the quality of the tree for its herbivore offspring.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of herbivory in the evolution of host phenology and its consequences for the synchrony of host and herbivore life cycles.
the influence of herbivory on the phenological response of a host plant and the impact of this response on the performance of a specialist folivorous insect.
the role of a herbivore in the evolution of phenology in its host plant.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
herbivory modifies the phenology of white spruce and that the induced amelioration improves the window for colonization of white spruce by Z. canandensis.
herbivory-induced amelioration by the specialist folivore Z. canadesis is an adaptive response that enhances the quality of white-spruce shoots for their offspring.
herbivory modifies the timing of bud development and bud burst in white spruce, which improves the window for colonization by Z. canadasensis and increases its fitness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
herbivory modifies the phenology of conifers, but that herbivores may be able to ameliorate the effects of their own herbivory by inducing a compensatory response in their host.
herbivory by a folivore modifies phenology and the pattern of herbivore colonisation of white pine.
herbivory by a specialist folvior modifies phenology of the host plant and improves the window for colonization by the herbivore.
The main takeaway from our work is that
herbivore induced changes in the timing of phenology can have important implications for plant–herbivore interactions.

herbivores can induce changes in the phenology (timing of bud burst) of their host plants and that these changes may be beneficial to the herbivore by improving the window of opportunity for colonization of the host.
the herbivore's ability to manipulate its host plant to its own benefit may be a key factor in the maintenance of a host-plant-specialist relationship.
